web_title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain, Pricing & Unit Economics
book_title: Chapter 3: How a Rupee Flows — Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics
question: How does Yash sell into utilities and OEMs, where are its supply-chain bottlenecks, and what does the audited FY26 unit-economics waterfall reveal?

epigraph.quote: Revenue is an engineering vanity metric until it clears working capital and turns into operating cash.
epigraph.author: Industrial Capital Allocation Rule

web_blocks.html: Yash sells through two B2B channels: Transformer OEMs and Direct Utilities/EPCs [1]. It serves 300+ global OEMs and over 1,000 utility customers across 60+ countries, including every Indian state utility and nuclear plant [1]. Utilities dictate approved bushing vendors inside their transformer tenders. Winning an OEM order therefore requires direct end-utility type-test approval, which takes 8 to 10 years [1]. Once approved, switching costs remain high and Yash retains a 96%+ repeat order rate [1]. Even so, headline breadth masks meaningful customer concentration: on the Q3 FY25 earnings call, management disclosed that its top-5 customers contribute ~40–45% of revenue (product-mix adjusted, and up to ~70% on narrower product slices), reflecting India's concentrated domestic transformer-OEM oligopoly.

Abroad, Yash pairs local technical reps with established grid distributors instead of building costly branches. In Europe and North Africa, Weidmann Electrical Technology AG exclusively represents Yash's OIP bushings (up to 245 kV) and HC units (up to 25 kA) [16]. In the United States—home to over 3,000 utilities—Yash HV USA Inc. signed 36-month deals with three regional partners [5]. These include ENSALES Electrical Associates (19 states), Gateway Power Sales (3 Midwestern states), and EHV Solutions LLC (5 Western/South-Central states) [5]. Together, they give Yash sales coverage across 27 US states as of October 2026 [5]. However, export orders remain early at ~₹40–50 crore (5–7% of the backlog), and trade-policy friction escalated on 25 November 2026 when the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) issued affirmative Section 301 determinations proposing additional tariffs of up to 25% on all goods of India (or 17% under a bilateral reciprocal trade agreement, versus 15% proposed caps for the EU, Switzerland, Japan, and Korea), subject to final annex exemptions after January 2027 hearings.

web_blocks.title: 3.2 Supply Chain, Import Dependency & Working Capital Cycle

web_blocks.html: Yash's bill of materials relies on electrical kraft and crepe paper, aluminum foil, epoxy resin, insulators, and copper or aluminum conductors. Historically, its biggest supply-chain bottleneck has been imported RIP capacitive cores [1]. Over 95% of RIP cores assembled in India come from Europe and China [1]. That dependency creates 12-to-16-week lead times, ~18–20% combined import duty and freight friction on core costs, and a steep currency mismatch: in FY26, foreign-exchange outflows totaled roughly ₹130.6 crore (~55.5% of revenue) against only ₹17.2 crore in export earnings, leaving a ~₹113.4 crore net FX deficit. Crucially, Yash's Swiss technology partner and former shareholder MGC Moser Glaser—whose equity stake Yash bought back in 2024—holds an Indian core-supply exclusivity window running only until mid-2027 with no non-compete bar, creating a firm operational deadline for Jarod's in-house core ramp.

That bottleneck explains why FY26 Cash Flow from Operations (CFO) trailed PAT. Revenue jumped 57% to ₹235.1 crore, so Yash raised buffer inventory from ₹29.7 crore (Mar-25) to ₹66.7 crore (Mar-26) [1][2]. That build pushed the FY26 Cash Conversion Cycle (CCC) to 81 days and absorbed ₹51.9 crore in working capital [1][2]. By H1 FY27, inventory stabilized at ₹71.8 crore on a ₹389 crore annualized run-rate [2]. Higher trade payables and customer advances compressed the CCC to 63 days, even as DSO rose temporarily from 47 to 66 days on Q2 billings [2]. Indigenous RIP/RIS core winding at Jarod in H2 FY27 will remove import duties and shorten lead times, though management noted it will continue importing cores during the transition until internal lines cover rising demand [1].

The waterfall below traces Yash Highvoltage's audited FY26 consolidated income statement [1]. It follows ₹235.1 crore of revenue down to ₹37.4 crore of Profit After Tax [1]. It also reconciles earnings to ₹8.82 crore of operating cash flow and ₹59.2 crore of greenfield capex [1].

web_blocks.title: 3.4 Pricing Power, Cost Structure & Operating Leverage

web_blocks.html: Yash's pricing is order-driven and backed by technical specs rather than spot commodities. Utility bushings have long lead times, and the ₹760 crore order book spans 15 to 20 months [1][2]. Yash quotes fixed or formula-adjusted prices that protect raw-material spreads and capture mix gains [1][2]. In FY26, material COGS took 53.3% of revenue (₹125.4 Cr on ₹235.1 Cr) [1]. Employee and direct labor costs took 11.2% (₹26.3 Cr), and other operating expenses took 12.3% (₹28.9 Cr) [1]. Operating EBITDA reached ₹54.5 Cr, or ₹60.4 Cr including ₹5.8 Cr of other income [1].

In H1 FY27, gross margin jumped +590 bps YoY from 42.4% to 48.3% (₹93.9 Cr on ₹194.5 Cr revenue) [1]. Employee costs fell from 11.2% (FY26) to 10.8% of revenue (₹21.0 Cr incl. direct labor) [1]. Other expenses settled at 13.6% (₹26.5 Cr incl. direct mfg), lifting EBITDA margin to 28.1% [1]. Once indigenous RIP core production scales at Jarod, Yash eliminates third-party core margins and the ~18–20% import duty and freight drag [1]. Management has cautioned, however, that competitive pricing and customer expectations will determine how much of that localization saving stays in EBITDA versus being shared to win export and domestic volume.

Localization also improves working-capital velocity. Importing RIP cores from Europe and China forces 12-to-16-week transit buffers and vendor advances whenever order intake spikes [1]. Producing those cores in Vadodara shortens lead times, reduces the ₹113.4 crore FY26 net FX outflow gap, and lowers work-in-progress inventory. Lower transit stock should help keep the Cash Conversion Cycle below 70 days as revenue scales [2].

book_paragraphs: If you want to know how a specialized industrial company actually makes money, follow two trails: who controls the specification sheet, and where the cash gets stuck between the factory gate and the bank account.

On the specification sheet, Yash sits in an enviable position. Even when a transformer manufacturer like CG Power or Hitachi Energy is building the transformer, the end customer—say, Power Grid Corporation or NTPC—dictates which bushing vendors are approved on the tender. Getting onto that approved vendor list takes eight to ten years of field testing and zero-defect performance. Once you are on it, however, transformer OEMs rarely switch to save a few percentage points on a component that represents a small fraction of the transformer's cost. That is why Yash's repeat order rate sits above 96%. Still, do not mistake a 300-OEM roster for fragmented demand: management disclosed on the Q3 FY25 call that its top five customers generate roughly 40% to 45% of revenue on a product-mix-adjusted basis (and up to 70% on narrower slices), tying near-term shipments tightly to India's largest transformer factories.

On the supply-chain trail, Yash has had one glaring structural vulnerability: its reliance on imported RIP capacitive cores from Europe and China. When you import the heart of your flagship product, you carry 12 to 16 weeks of shipping lead time, pay roughly 18% to 20% in combined import duties and freight, and run a massive foreign-exchange deficit—₹130.6 crore of FX spending in FY26 against just ₹17.2 crore of export receipts. Worse, Swiss partner MGC Moser Glaser, whose former equity stake Yash bought back in 2024, supplies cores exclusively in India only until mid-2027 with no non-compete bar. You can see that supply-chain friction in the FY26 numbers: Yash earned ₹37.4 crore in net profit on ₹235.1 crore of revenue, yet operating cash flow was only ₹8.82 crore because inventory more than doubled from ₹29.7 crore to ₹66.7 crore.

book_subsections.title: Reading the Cash Conversion Turnaround in H1 FY27
paragraphs: What separates a disciplined operator from an inventory-bloated manufacturer is what happens next. In H1 FY27, even as revenue surged 95% year-on-year to ₹194.5 crore, Yash held inventory nearly flat at ₹71.8 crore, brought its cash conversion cycle down from 81 days to 63 days, and generated ₹45.2 crore in operating cash flow—125% of net profit. Crucially, part of that cash surge came from higher trade payables and customer advances offsetting rising receivables, so repeatability over H2 FY27 remains a live test.

Now watch what happens as the Jarod greenfield facility commissions in the second half of FY27. By winding and impregnating RIP/RIS cores in-house before Moser Glaser's mid-2027 exclusivity sunset, Yash removes import duties, air/sea freight, and months of transit inventory in a single stroke—while enabling RIP exports to Europe and the Americas for the first time.

callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
callouts.text: The FY26 CFO dip to ₹8.82 crore was a working-capital growth tax, not earnings fragility—proven when H1 FY27 CFO snapped back to ₹45.2 crore. Still, keep a close eye on receivable days (up from 47 to 66 days in H1 FY27) and the hard mid-2027 clock on Swiss core supply.

book_subsections.title: Why Localization at Jarod Changes Both Margins and Working Capital
paragraphs: To understand the strategic logic of the ₹220 crore Jarod greenfield plant, put yourself in the shoes of Yash's procurement head over the past five years. When more than 95% of India's RIP capacitive cores are imported from Europe and China, every surge in domestic demand forces you to place core orders 12 to 16 weeks in advance, pay roughly 18% to 20% in customs duties and freight, post vendor advances, and sit on elevated work-in-progress inventory.

Worse still, you cannot competitively export RIP bushings to Europe or North America if you are buying the core from Europe, flying it to Gujarat, assembling it, and shipping it back out. By installing Swiss and German winding and resin-impregnation lines inside Jarod—with Phase 1 assembly already generating its first invoice on 30 September 2026 and full end-to-end core production commissioning in Q3 FY27—Yash turns a supply-chain bottleneck into a cost and lead-time advantage, even if some of that 18–20% cost relief is shared with customers to win share.

book_subsections.title: Distribution Leverage Meets US Tariff Friction
paragraphs: Look at how Yash approaches international distribution. Rather than hiring dozens of salaried salespeople across Europe and the United States—which would bloat fixed SG&A ahead of revenue—Yash partnered with Weidmann Electrical Technology AG in Europe and North Africa, and built a commission-aligned representation network across 27 US states through ENSALES Electrical Associates, Gateway Power Sales, and EHV Solutions LLC.

That structure keeps fixed overhead low while putting Yash's technical catalog in front of more than 3,000 American utilities through local engineers who already know the regional utility buyers. Yet the November 2026 trade-policy turn introduces a new variable: on 25 November 2026, the U.S. Trade Representative proposed Section 301 tariffs of up to 25% on all Indian goods (17% under a bilateral trade agreement, versus 15% caps for Europe and Switzerland), pending January 2027 hearings and product-exemption lists. Unless transformer bushings win annex exemptions or India secures a lower reciprocal rate, US tariffs could absorb part of the 30–40% export realization premium Yash expects as US orders convert in FY28.
